Figure 36 (Left) High voltage PTR electron beam welder operated by Aerie Aerospace, Huntsville Alabama [71] (Center) Sciaky EBW with additive manufacturing capabilities hosted at NASA Langley Research Center with a 7’ x 7’ x 9’ chamber[72] (Right) Electron beam welding of 201MHz copper cavity for MICE experiment performed at NASA-Langley In 1994, NASA was faced with significant budget cuts from the Clinton Administration which included sweeping organizational changes to cut spending by $5 billion by the end of the decade, which would be taken as reductions of the FY96 budget by -3%, -5%, -7% and -9% for years FY97-FY00 [73]]. This initiative kicked-off an internal review process referred to as the "Zero-Base Review," which streamlined functions amongst facilities such that each site became a center of excellence concentrated on a specific aspects of NASA's mission. Another objective of ZBR was to reduce overlap and consolidate administrative and program functions across NASA. This efficiency drive eventually led to the creation of the NASA ‘Fabrication Alliance’ which provided a formal contracting and communication forum to share specialized manufacturing capabilities as well as generalized manufacturing capacity between facilities. [74] Manufacturing at NASA centers often includes complex, one-off prototypes and components which do not lend themselves to efficiency. Initially beginning with 4 research centers related to the Office of Aeronautics & Space Transportation Technology, the Fabrication Alliance evolved to include all 10 NASA field centers[74]. A guiding principle of the Fabrication Alliance remains: Cooperation, Not Competition and aims to foster personal relationships and trust amongst the centers. Project deliverables included agreements to standardize certain software packages, generating a computer tracking system for sharing excess materials and equipment amongst facilities and the generation of a single-unified contract for obtaining outside fabrication services. Additionally, participants agreed to limit and share specialized fabrication capabilities. For instance, Goddard Space flight center had developed unique metal plating capabilities which now became easily available across the Agency through the Fabrication Alliance. Mechanisms for inter-facility payment were also established using both ad hoc and formal approaches. Defense-Focused: Dynetics Technical Solutions (DTS) recently acquired a 22’ x 22’ x 22’ internal gun system from Germany to support government and commercial programs at both the unclassified and classified levels [75]. Primary usage of the equipment is for fabrication of Virginia and Columbia class submarine hardware as well as in support of the U.S. Army’s Long Range Hypersonic Weapons program. This welder complements DTS’s 20’ x 7’ x 7’ EBW from the same manufacturer as well as over 30 CNC machining centers in support of large structural hardware pre and post weld machining.
